lesson.title: When the Real World Asks for Two Answers
lesson.summary: Applications of quadratics use the same set up strategy as linear word problems, define a variable and translate the situation into an equation, but the equation is quadratic whenever the problem involves a product of two related unknown quantities.
lesson.body:
Setting up a quadratic word problem follows the same first steps as setting up a linear one: read carefully, choose a variable for the unknown quantity, and translate the words into an equation. What changes is why the equation becomes quadratic instead of linear. Linear applications usually involve a quantity that changes at a constant rate or is combined by addition. Quadratic applications typically involve multiplying two quantities that both depend on the same unknown, such as length times width for an area, or price times quantity sold for a revenue, which produces an x^2 term once you substitute an expression for one of the two factors.

There is one habit that matters more here than in linear problems: always check candidate solutions against the real world context, not just against the equation. A quadratic equation typically produces two solutions, but a length, a width, a time, or a price cannot be negative, so one of the two mathematically valid solutions is often physically meaningless and must be discarded.

Consider a rectangular garden whose length is 3 feet more than its width, with a total area of 40 square feet. Let w stand for the width in feet, so the length is w + 3. Since area is length times width, w(w + 3) = 40, which expands to w^2 + 3w = 40, or w^2 + 3w - 40 = 0 once everything is moved to one side. This factors by looking for two numbers that multiply to -40 and add to 3, which are 8 and -5: (w + 8)(w - 5) = 0. Setting each factor to zero gives w = -8 or w = 5. A width of -8 feet makes no sense for a garden, so it is discarded, leaving w = 5. The length is then w + 3 = 8. Checking against the original problem, 5 feet times 8 feet is 40 square feet, matching exactly.

Not every applied quadratic factors as cleanly as this one. When the numbers in a real problem do not produce a nice factorization, the same setup strategy still applies, define the variable, write the equation, and solve, only the last step switches to completing the square or the quadratic formula from earlier chapters instead of factoring by inspection. The setup is the genuinely new skill here. Once an application is correctly translated into a quadratic equation, every tool from the earlier chapters is available to actually solve it.
